findings.title: Recovery codes stored in user storage are never consumed / exhaustion is never detected
findings.body: After a successful validation the authenticator now resolves the credential via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(), which prefers the credential returned by the user-storage provider (getFederatedCredentialsStream). A federated credential model is rebuilt on every request from the raw code list, so its "next code" index and remaining-code counter are always reset: allCodesUsed() can never become true, the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is never re-added, and the login form always asks for code #0 again. In addition, removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()) is called with an id that belongs to (or is null for) the user-storage credential, so it cannot delete anything from local storage. Practically this means a single recovery code can be replayed indefinitely for federated users, defeating the one-time-use property of recovery codes. Either the consumption must be delegated to the storage provider through a defined contract, or the codes must be kept (and marked used) in local storage.

findings.title: Mock user storage validates recovery codes without consuming them
findings.body: isValid() for RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE matches the submitted code against the stored list and returns true, but never removes/marks the code as used and never updates the stored credential. The same code (and every other code) therefore stays valid forever. Since this provider is the reference implementation used by the new test, it encodes the wrong semantics for recovery codes (which must be single-use) and makes the test pass even though replay is possible.

findings.title: getCredentials() can NPE and drops the credential id
findings.body: `var myUser = getMyUser(user);` is dereferenced at line 235 without the null check used by every other method in this class (isConfiguredFor, getDisableableCredentialTypesStream), so a lookup for a user that is no longer present in the in-memory map throws a NullPointerException instead of returning an empty stream. Furthermore, the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel built by createFromValues() does not carry the stored credential id (myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()), so callers such as RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator (which calls removeStoredCredentialById(model.getId())) and the account/admin credential listing receive a credential with a null id and cannot reference or delete it.

findings.title: User label and generation time are lost when codes are stored in user storage
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential() only passes type + JSON of raw codes to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(new UserCredentialModel("", type, json)). The fully populated RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel (user label entered in the required-action form, generatedAt timestamp, remaining code counter) is used only on the local-storage fallback path. For federated users this metadata is silently dropped, so the stored credential has no label/creation date and the account console cannot display the information the user supplied. The storage provider also has no way to know how many codes remain.

findings.title: No verification or cleanup after delegating recovery-code creation to user storage
findings.body: The method treats a `true` return from updateCredential() as success and then skips local creation entirely, without verifying that the credential is actually usable (unlike createOTPCredential, which calls isValid afterwards) and without removing any pre-existing local recovery-codes credential. A storage provider that returns true from updateCredential for this type but does not persist the codes would leave the user with no working recovery codes even though the required action reports success; and if a local credential already existed, it stays in the DB while RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() always prefers the federated one, leaving a stale, still-valid set of codes in local storage.

findings.title: Optional.get() without presence check leads to server error
findings.body: credentialModelOpt.get() is called unconditionally. If neither the user storage nor local storage returns a recovery-codes credential (e.g. the credential was removed between authenticator selection and form rendering, or the storage provider fails to deserialize it as in BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials where an IOException just logs and returns nothing), this throws NoSuchElementException while building the login form, producing an internal server error page instead of a proper authentication error.

findings.title: Login assertion incomplete and no coverage of code consumption/reuse
findings.body: Unlike testOTPUpdateAndLogin, this test never calls testAppHelper.completeLogin() after submitting the recovery code, so the authorization code is never exchanged; the subsequent testAppHelper.logout() result is also ignored (other tests wrap it in assertTrue), meaning a failed logout goes unnoticed. More importantly the test only performs a single login with code #0 and never verifies the core property of recovery codes: that the used code is rejected on a second login and that the next requested index advances. With the user-storage path this currently does not happen, so the gap hides a real regression.

findings.title: Unrelated 'delayed-authenticator' execution copied into the test flow
findings.body: configureBrowserFlowWithRecoveryAuthnCodes adds a REQUIRED "delayed-authenticator" execution (with the misspelled alias "delayed-suthenticator-config" and delay 0) into the browser flow used by testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin. This authenticator has nothing to do with recovery codes; it only couples the new test to another testsuite provider and will break flow creation if that provider is not deployed. The parameter `delay` is always 0, so it adds no value.

findings.title: Possible NPE on null credential type and no support for disabling recovery codes
findings.body: supportsCredentialType() uses `credentialType.equals(RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE)` (same pattern at line 275 in isConfiguredFor), which throws NullPointerException for a null credentialType, while the surrounding checks are written null-safely (`CredentialModel.PASSWORD.equals(credentialType)`). Additionally, disableCredentialType() and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream() were not extended for the new type, so a recovery-codes credential created in this storage can never be disabled/removed via admin or account REST.
